vocabulary.definition: A form of government where the monarch holds supreme autocratic authority, not being restricted by written laws, legislature, or customs.
A system of government in which a monarch shares power with a constitutionally organized government, often limited to ceremonial duties.
A political and religious doctrine asserting that a monarch is subject to no earthly authority, deriving the right to rule directly from the will of God.
The act of a monarch formally giving up their monarchical authority and status.
A person appointed to administer a state because the monarch is a minor, is absent, or is incapacitated.
A sequence of rulers from the same family, usually in the context of a feudal or monarchical system.
The spouse of a reigning monarch.
A period when normal government is suspended, especially between successive reigns or regimes.
An heir whose claim cannot be set aside by the birth of another heir.
The combination of two or more states that have the same monarch while their boundaries, laws, and interests remain distinct.
A rule of succession in some European monarchies that excluded females from the line of succession to the throne.
The ceremony of crowning a sovereign or a sovereign's consort.

timeline.event: Henry VII wins the Battle of Bosworth Field, establishing the Tudor Dynasty in England.
Charles V becomes King of Spain, later uniting the Spanish and Holy Roman Empires.
Elizabeth I ascends to the English throne, beginning the Elizabethan Era.
Louis XIV becomes King of France, eventually becoming the longest-reigning sovereign monarch in history.
Execution of Charles I of England following the English Civil War.
The Glorious Revolution sees William III and Mary II replace James II as joint monarchs of England.
Death of Louis XIV, the 'Sun King', marking the end of the height of French absolutism.
The French Revolution begins, leading to the eventual execution of Louis XVI.
The Congress of Vienna restores many European monarchies after the defeat of Napoleon.
Queen Victoria ascends to the British throne, beginning a 63-year reign.
Tsar Nicholas II of Russia abdicates amidst the Russian Revolution, ending the Romanov dynasty.
Elizabeth II becomes Queen of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms.

artworks.title: Portrait of Henry VIII
artworks.description: A commanding painting by Hans Holbein the Younger depicting a Tudor king in a confident, wide-legged stance, symbolizing aggressive masculinity and power.

artworks.title: Las Meninas
artworks.description: A complex composition by Diego Velázquez portraying the young Infanta Margarita Teresa and her entourage in the Spanish court, blurring reality and illusion.

artworks.title: The Coronation of Napoleon
artworks.description: A massive painting by Jacques-Louis David showing the new Emperor crowning his wife Josephine in Notre Dame Cathedral, legitimizing his self-made rule.

artworks.title: The Prince
artworks.description: A written work by Niccolò Machiavelli that argues rulers should prioritize stability and power over traditional morality, famously asking if it is better to be loved or feared.

artworks.title: Leviathan
artworks.description: Thomas Hobbes' influential work arguing for a social contract and rule by an absolute sovereign to prevent the 'war of all against all'.

artworks.title: Marie Antoinette with a Rose
artworks.description: A portrait by Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun intended to soften the public image of the French Queen, showing her in a formal yet gentle pose with a flower.

locations.name: Palace of Versailles
locations.significance: The primary residence of French kings from Louis XIV to Louis XVI, symbolizing the absolute power of the Ancien Régime.

locations.name: The Tower of London
locations.significance: A historic fortress used as a royal residence and a prison for high-profile figures like Anne Boleyn.

locations.name: Westminster Abbey
locations.significance: The traditional site of coronations and burials for English and British monarchs.

locations.name: El Escorial
locations.significance: A vast complex in Spain serving as a royal palace, monastery, and burial place for the King of Spain.

locations.name: The Winter Palace
locations.significance: The official residence of the Russian monarchs in St. Petersburg until the Russian Revolution.

locations.name: Schönbrunn Palace
locations.significance: The main summer residence of the Habsburg rulers in Vienna, Austria.

locations.name: Hampton Court Palace
locations.significance: A favorite residence of Henry VIII, originally built for Cardinal Wolsey before being seized by the King.

locations.name: Sanssouci
locations.significance: The summer palace of Frederick the Great, King of Prussia, located in Potsdam and famous for its Rococo style.

locations.name: Windsor Castle
locations.significance: The oldest and largest occupied castle in the world, a residence of British monarchs for nearly 1,000 years.

locations.name: Fotheringhay Castle
locations.significance: The site where Mary, Queen of Scots, was tried and executed in 1587.

trueFalse.statement: Louis XIV was known as the 'Moon King' because of his nocturnal habits.
trueFalse.correction: He was known as the 'Sun King' (le Roi Soleil) because he saw himself as the center of the nation.

trueFalse.statement: Queen Victoria wore black mourning clothes for forty years after the death of her husband, Prince Albert.
trueFalse.correction: She remained in mourning for the rest of her life after Albert died in 1861.
Henry VIII had six wives: Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard, and Catherine Parr.

trueFalse.statement: The Habsburg jaw was a physical condition resulting from generations of royal inbreeding.
trueFalse.correction: It refers to the mandibular prognathism prominent in the Habsburg family.

trueFalse.statement: Tsar Nicholas II was the first ruler of the Romanov dynasty.
trueFalse.correction: Nicholas II was the last Emperor of Russia; the dynasty began with Michael I in 1613.

trueFalse.statement: The War of the Spanish Succession was fought to prevent the union of the French and Spanish thrones.
trueFalse.correction: European powers feared the imbalance of power if the Bourbons controlled both France and Spain.

trueFalse.statement: Catherine the Great was born a Russian princess.
trueFalse.correction: She was born a German princess named Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst.

trueFalse.statement: The execution of Charles I led to the establishment of the Commonwealth of England under Oliver Cromwell.
trueFalse.correction: The monarchy was abolished from 1649 until the Restoration in 1660.

trueFalse.statement: Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon are known as the Catholic Monarchs.
trueFalse.correction: Their marriage unified Spain and they were granted the title by the Pope.

trueFalse.statement: King George III is best known for voluntarily giving independence to the American colonies.
trueFalse.correction: He opposed American independence, which was achieved through the Revolutionary War.

trueFalse.statement: Elizabeth I never married and was known as the 'Virgin Queen'.
trueFalse.correction: She used her single status as a diplomatic tool throughout her reign.

trueFalse.statement: Napoleon Bonaparte was born into the French Royal family.
trueFalse.correction: Napoleon was from a minor noble family in Corsica and seized power after the French Revolution.
